summary:
Same-sex relations are legal nationwide in Romania. Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, though institutional follow-through is limited. There is no same-sex marriage and no civil union: the 2018 constitutional referendum that would have written a ban into the constitution failed on low turnout, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill tabled since 2017. LGBTI organisations can register and operate.

Legal gender recognition exists and is obtained through the courts, but civil-status authorities resist it in practice. The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in October 2024, reported by Reuters, that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition in Romania of a United Kingdom gender recognition certificate.

In that case the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates, making the decision definitive in March 2026. ACCEPT Romania announced the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who have changed their documents in another European Union member state to pursue transcription in Romania.

Official rhetoric is a documented risk factor. During the 2025 presidential campaign, candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself "against LGBTQ" in February and Prime Minister Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes. The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride "provocation" framing after a complaint by ACCEPT, and a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

Protection machinery exists and is recorded as uneven. The Council of Europe published a national thematic review in January 2023 on hate crimes and other hate-motivated incidents against LGBTI people, covering the legal and policy framework, applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law and international standards. ACCEPT Romania authored the Romania chapter of the 2025 Rule of Law Report submissions, which identifies the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

Visible assembly takes place under visible hostility. In June 2025 the Bucharest pride march marked its twentieth anniversary with tens of thousands of participants, AP reporting, against a backdrop of growing right-wing hostility toward LGBTQ+ Romanians.
tangentialFactors:
Of the nine country submissions to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, which places Romania's election-period surge within a wider regional pattern rather than an isolated episode.

Public opinion is more permissive than the legislative record suggests. The IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found that 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition, while no partnership law has been enacted.

A FRA-commissioned legal study by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu, published in February 2008, maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners, including national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints. It is a dated baseline for the protection architecture rather than a current statement of it.
localsOnly:
Government Ordinance 137/2000 covers both sex and sexual orientation, and enforcement runs through the National Council for Combating Discrimination (CNCD), which holds investigative powers and receives complaints from NGOs. Outright International's Romania overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that institutional follow-through on this framework is limited.

The CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials, an instance of the council acting on commercial refusal of advocacy output rather than on individual complaints.

March 2024 drafts of education legislation carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew protests from 13 religious groups and a counter-response from organisations representing more than 50 signatories, indicating the domestic contest over how anti-discrimination rules are taught.

The 2018 referendum on constitutionally barring same-sex marriage failed on low turnout, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017, so residents have neither marriage nor a registered-partnership route. LGBTI organisations can register as associations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source entry or visa screening practice, including whether gender markers on passports are checked at the border or whether screening could disclose a visitor's trans status. This remains unresolved.

No sourced material addresses detention or prison placement policy for trans detainees, facilities and bathroom access, or continuity of hormone treatment and other care for a visitor. These are not covered by the sources and are not stated either way.

The Council of Europe's January 2023 thematic review is identified as a national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, but its findings, recommendations and any follow-up are not reproduced in the inventory; the substance of that review remains unresolved here.

Whether the Mirzarafie-Ahi transcription has been applied to other cases, and how frequently civil-status directorates continue to resist, is not sourced beyond the single case. Hate-crime recording and conviction outcomes for LGBTI victims are likewise not quantified in the available material.
